To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) stocks are not less risky the longer they are held; (2) the risk of stocks does not decline with their maturity; (3) stocks are more risky than bonds for guarantors of fixed annuities.

(i) stocks are a better hedge against long run risk the shorter the time horizon of the investor, and (ii) stocks are a worse hedge against long run risks for annuitants the longer the maturity date of their obligations.
the risk of a portfolio of common stocks is not lower the longer the investor plans to hold the portfolio, and the risk of a stock is not a good hedge against the risk of a money fixed annuity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long run properties and the long term risks of stock returns, not with short term fluctuations in stock prices.
the risk of stocks in the long run and with the proposition that the risk of stocks declines as the length of time an investor plans to keep them increases.
the proposition that the risk of common stock investments declines with the length of time that the investment is to be held.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stocks are not less risky the longer the investment horizon.
, in the long run, common stocks are not less risky than other investments.
the long run properties are not important in determining the riskiness of stocks in a given investment portfolio.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stocks are riskier the longer you hold them.
the long run properties are not the only ones that matter.
the proposition that stocks are less risky the longer the horizon of the investment is not correct.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the long run properties (or lack thereof) of stock returns have no implications for the risk of investing in stocks in the long run.

the long run properties that are most relevant to investors are the properties of the returns that they actually earn over the long run, not the properties of the long run returns that they could have earned had they held the same portfolio for a longer period.
